headline: Himlung avalanche killed 15 Nepali crew, and fellow guides dug out the dead
dek: All 16 buried were Nepali guides and cooks. An NNMGA team of about ten went back in after the first search stopped for lack of hands.
body_markdown:
Nepal's confirmed death toll from the Himlung Himal avalanche reached 15 on Thursday, October 1, after search teams recovered eight more bodies at the mountain's base camp in Manang district. One worker remains missing, Krishna Prasad Paudel, assistant chief district officer of Manang, told reporters that day.

All 16 people buried were Nepali high altitude workers, not foreign climbers. They were guides and kitchen staff from two companies, Himalayan Holidays Trek and Expedition and Imagine Nepal, sent ahead of their foreign clients to fix ropes and pitch camp for the autumn climbing season, Kathmandu Post reported. They are the workforce that cooks, carries and builds the camps so foreign climbers can summit. No foreign climbers were on the mountain when the snow hit. The first search for them stopped on September 29, ActionHub and The Star reported, because an eight person team did not have enough hands to keep digging.

The avalanche struck before dawn on Sunday, September 27, burying tents at the 7,126 metre peak's base camp under as much as four metres of snow, the Nepal National Mountain Guide Association, Nepal's climbing guides' body known as NNMGA, said. The Star reported two bodies were found that Sunday and two more on Monday. By Tuesday, September 29, NNMGA suspended the search. "With only eight people on scene, our manpower wasn't enough to continue the search," association president Tul Singh Gurung said. A new team resumed the search on September 30 at the request of victims' families and Himalayan Holidays Trek and Expedition, recovering three bodies, then eight more on October 1, airlifted by Nepali Army helicopter to Chame and Phu village.

## What the coverage missed

Kathmandu Post, Xinhua and the Associated Press carried the toll of 15 on October 1 and 2.

The team that dug out the final eight bodies was not a state disaster unit. It was organized by NNMGA, the same association that had suspended the search two days earlier for lack of manpower. The Nepal Army flew recovered bodies to Chame and Phu village by helicopter on October 1, Radio Nepal Online reported. The digging was carried out by an NNMGA team of about ten guides, Radio Nepal Online reported. No outlet reviewed for this piece reported Army or Armed Police Force personnel joining the digging.

Nepal has no dedicated state mountain rescue system, Nepalnews reported in an analysis of the country's mountaineering safety gaps. The outlet quoted Angbabu Sherpa, an executive committee member of the Nepal Mountaineering Association, saying climbers and expedition companies ask each other to carry out rescues when accidents happen, which doubles costs for companies whose staff have to stop climbing to help.

The first count of missing after the avalanche never settled quickly. Manang's Chief District Officer, Mukti Prasad Khanal, said on September 27 that 12 of a 22 person group were feared missing, Rising Nepal Daily reported. By September 28, once all 16 affected workers were confirmed, NNMGA cited 12 missing after four bodies had been found.

## What we still do not know

Whether the Nepal Army or Armed Police Force did anything beyond fly recovered bodies by helicopter, or whether the entire digging operation was left to NNMGA's guides, is something Nepal Army's public relations directorate or NNMGA could answer.

Whether the 16 workers were insured, and who will compensate their families, is something the two companies, Manang's district administration or Nepal's Social Security Fund could answer.

The identity of the one worker still missing, and whether his family has been publicly named, is something Manang's district administration or NNMGA could answer.

key_facts.fact: Nepal's confirmed toll from the Himlung Himal avalanche reached 15 dead, with one worker still missing, on Thursday, October 1, after eight more bodies were recovered.
A 1News report dated October 3 presented the toll of 15 as new, though Kathmandu Post, Xinhua and the Associated Press had already reported the same figure on October 1 and 2.
All 16 people buried in the avalanche were Nepali guides and kitchen staff from two companies, Himalayan Holidays and Imagine Nepal, not foreign climbers.
The Nepal National Mountain Guide Association suspended its search on September 29, with its president Tul Singh Gurung saying an eight person team's manpower was not enough to continue.
Bodies recovered on October 1 were airlifted by a Nepali Army helicopter to Chame and Phu village, while the digging was carried out by an NNMGA team of about ten guides, Radio Nepal Online reported.
Initial missing counts fluctuated, with Manang's Chief District Officer saying on September 27 that 12 of a 22 person group were feared missing, before the total of 16 affected workers was confirmed.

social_hook: The 16 workers buried on Himlung were Nepali guides and kitchen staff, not foreign climbers, the backbone of every expedition that heads up Nepal's mountains.
take: Sixteen Nepali workers were buried at Himlung base camp, guides and kitchen staff sent ahead of foreign clients, not foreign climbers. Nepal's toll hit 15 dead, one missing, last Thursday, confirmed by Manang's assistant CDO Krishna Prasad Paudel. The eight bodies that pushed the count that high were dug out by an NNMGA team of about ten guides, the same association that had already given up once for lack of manpower, its president Tul Singh Gurung said. The Nepal Army flew the dead out, Radio Nepal Online reported. No outlet has reported it joined the digging. Nepal has no dedicated state mountain rescue system, Nepalnews reported.

caption.body:
Eight more bodies were pulled from Himlung Himal's base camp on October 1, raising the toll to 15, with one worker still missing, Manang's assistant CDO Krishna Prasad Paudel said.

All 16 victims were Nepali guides and kitchen staff, not foreign climbers, sent ahead to fix ropes and pitch camp for the autumn season.

The first search stopped once for lack of manpower, Nepal National Mountain Guide Association president Tul Singh Gurung said. An NNMGA team of about ten guides did the digging, Radio Nepal Online reported. The Nepal Army flew the bodies out. No outlet has reported soldiers digging.

One worker is still missing, Manang officials said.
caption.trigger: When the search team ran short of hands, guides went back for their own. Should the state run its own mountain rescue team, or should expedition companies pay for it?

angles.claim: The '15 dead' toll that the candidate 1News story (Oct 3) reports as a fresh jump had already been established and widely reported by Nepali and international outlets by October 1-2, roughly two days earlier.
angles.why_it_matters: A newsroom built on being 'checked before it reaches you' should frame this as an update to Nepal Wire's own earlier count of seven dead/nine missing, dated to October 1 when the toll actually moved, not present a two-day-old wire figure as today's news.

evidence.fact: Rescuers discovered eight bodies at the base camp of Mount Himlung in Nepal on Thursday, raising the total number of deaths to 15, in a story published October 2, 2026.
The death toll from an avalanche...has risen to 15 after eight more bodies were recovered on Thursday, while one person remains missing, published 01 Oct 2026, 8:19 PM.
Ekantipur's October 1, 2026 headline already reports the toll reaching 15 with one person still missing.
Rescuers recovered eight more bodies on Thursday from the area of the avalanche...in one of the worst mountain disasters in recent years, published October 2, 2026.

angles.claim: Body recovery at Himlung was carried out by a roughly eight-to-eleven-person volunteer team organized by the Nepal National Mountain Guide Association (NNMGA), which had already suspended the search once for lack of manpower, while Nepal's Tourism Act 1978 places legal responsibility for mountaineering rescues and compensation on private expedition operators rather than the state, even as the government collects large sums from climbing royalties.
angles.why_it_matters: For a disaster that killed Nepali support staff rather than foreign clients, this raises a question mainstream coverage has not asked: why a state that profits heavily from mountaineering permits left recovery at 7,126 metres to an under-resourced volunteer association.

evidence.fact: A team of eleven rescuers, including experienced guides, were at the site, digging through more than four metres (14 feet) of snow.

evidence.source: ActionHub, quoting NNMGA president Tul Singh Gurung
evidence.fact: "With only eight people on scene, our manpower wasn't enough to continue the search," association president Tul Singh Gurung said, describing the September 29-30 suspension.

For granting permits to 1,070 climbers across 29 mountains in spring 2026 alone, the government collected USD 1.17 billion solely from royalties, while the Tourism Act of 1978 stipulates that expedition teams themselves must handle rescues and provide compensation if an uninsured worker dies.

angles.claim: In the first 24-48 hours after the avalanche, three different bodies gave three different missing-person counts: the Expedition Operators Association Nepal said 10, the Nepal National Mountain Guide Association and Kathmandu Post said 14, and other wire reports said 12 -- a discrepancy that was never publicly reconciled.
angles.why_it_matters: If the base count itself was unsettled from day one, presenting the move to '15 dead, one missing' as a clean, single jump risks repeating a number that officials and industry bodies themselves never agreed on.

evidence.source: Kathmandu Post/Daily Pioneer, quoting Rishi Bhandari
evidence.fact: Rishi Bhandari, general secretary of the Expedition Operators Association Nepal, told The Kathmandu Post that two of the missing are associated with Imagine Nepal Pvt Ltd and eight with Himalayan Holidays Nepal.
A 14-member rescue team was deployed to search for 14 Nepali high-altitude workers and guides who went missing after an avalanche on Himlung Himal.
The exact number of people missing has varied in initial reports. The Kathmandu Post reported that 14 people were unaccounted for, while other reports put the number at around 10 to 12.

angles.claim: This is the deadliest disaster for Nepali high-altitude support workers since the 2014 Khumbu Icefall avalanche, which killed 16 Sherpas and led to disputes over inadequate government compensation and mandatory insurance; it is not yet reported whether the Labour Act's mandatory 700,000-rupee accident insurance will be paid to the Himlung victims' families, and Himlung itself already had one unresolved rescue-insurance dispute involving an altitude limit the year before.
angles.why_it_matters: Families of the dead and other high-altitude workers have a direct financial stake in whether Nepal's insurance and compensation system performs better in 2026 than it did in 2014, when Sherpas called the government's initial relief offer inadequate.

evidence.fact: The employer shall procure accidental insurance of at least seven hundred thousand rupees covering all kinds of accidents for each labour, and if the labour dies as a result of an accident, the legal heir shall get compensation from that insurance.
The Nepalese government announced compensation of Nepali Rs. 40,000 ($400) each as immediate relief to the victims' next of kin, an offering that only covered funeral costs and angered Sherpas.
Nepal's mountaineers have threatened to stop work in seven days unless compensation of $10,000 is paid to the families of colleagues killed, injured or missing.

The current accident recalls a death that occurred on Himlung during a major storm last year, involving issues with the insurance company, which alleged the climber was stranded above the altitude limit of helicopters.

unanswered.question: Did the Nepal Army, Armed Police Force or any state disaster-response agency join the recovery effort at any point, or was the entire operation carried out by the roughly eight-to-eleven-person volunteer NNMGA team that reporting describes?
unanswered.who_could_answer: Nepal Army public relations directorate, Ministry of Home Affairs, NNMGA president Tul Singh Gurung

unanswered.question: Were the 16 workers caught in the avalanche covered by the mandatory 700,000-rupee accident insurance required under Section 55 of the Labour Act, and if any were not, will the expedition companies pay compensation directly as the Tourism Act requires for uninsured workers?
unanswered.who_could_answer: Himalayan Holidays Nepal, Imagine Nepal Treks, Department of Tourism, Social Security Fund

unanswered.question: Why did the Expedition Operators Association Nepal (10 missing), the Nepal National Mountain Guide Association/Kathmandu Post (14 missing) and other wire reports (12 missing) give different missing-person counts in the first 24-48 hours, and which figure did officials ultimately treat as authoritative?
unanswered.who_could_answer: Expedition Operators Association Nepal (Rishi Bhandari), NNMGA (Tul Singh Gurung), Manang district administration

unanswered.question: What happened to the 14-member UAE student climbing group that Himalayan Holidays Nepal was reportedly preparing the camp for, who were scheduled to arrive October 1 -- were they notified before departure, rerouted, or is their expedition cancelled?
unanswered.who_could_answer: Himalayan Holidays Nepal, the UAE school or program that organized the trip

unanswered.question: Who is the current, confirmed single missing person, and has that individual's identity and family been named by any official source, or does privacy require withholding it?
unanswered.who_could_answer: Manang Chief District Officer's office, NNMGA

investigation.summary: Nepal Wire can tell readers that the '15 dead' toll the wider press is treating as new on October 3 had already circulated via AP, Al Jazeera and Nepali outlets since October 1-2, and should be framed as an update to our own October 1 count rather than today's news. It can also report what others have not: the recovery was run by a roughly eight-to-eleven-person volunteer guides' association that had already suspended its search once for lack of manpower, under a Tourism Act that puts rescue and compensation duties on private operators even as the state collects over a billion dollars a season in climbing royalties, and that early missing-person counts (10, 12, and 14) were never publicly reconciled.

ranking.reason: Real development since our October 1 piece: the toll moved from seven dead and nine missing to 15 dead and one missing. Kathmandu Post, AP and Rising Nepal confirm it, and Rising Nepal attributes it to Assistant CDO Paudel, so the writer must use the official figure and frame it as an update to our own count, not a scoop. Weakest dimension is comment friction.

Confirmed. Our October 1 piece said seven dead and nine missing. Kathmandu Post, AP and Rising Nepal now report 15 dead and one missing, which still sums to the same 16 Nepali workers, and Rising Nepal attributes the count to Assistant CDO Paudel. The writer must date the rise to October 1, as Kathmandu Post does, and frame it as an update to our own count, not news from today. Weakest dimension is comment friction.

findings.passage: but the digging through metres of snow fell to roughly ten volunteer guides.
findings.problem: This is stated as settled fact in the 'What the coverage missed' section, the dek ('volunteer guides did the digging, not the state'), the take, the caption and the card headline. Yet the article's own 'What we still do not know' section admits: 'Whether the Nepal Army or Armed Police Force did anything beyond fly recovered bodies by helicopter, or whether the entire digging operation was left to volunteer guides, is something Nepal Army's public relations directorate or NNMGA could answer.' The piece asserts as proven exactly what it elsewhere says it cannot confirm.
findings.suggested_fix: Pick one position. If Nepal Army/APF involvement beyond flying is genuinely unconfirmed, strip the declarative claim from the dek, body, take, caption and card headline and replace with attributed, hedged language: 'Radio Nepal Online reported the Army flew bodies out; no outlet has reported it joined the digging.' Do not present an open question as a closed fact anywhere else in the piece.

findings.problem: The card headline states a conduct claim (the Army did not dig) in flat declarative voice. Per the card headline standard, an unproven conduct claim must carry a status signal or be framed as a question, not run declarative. The article's own unanswered-questions section shows this is not proven. This headline will circulate alone as a screenshot and could be read as a factual indictment of the Nepal Army that the record does not establish.
findings.suggested_fix: Rewrite as an open question or hedge it: 'DID THE ARMY ONLY FLY?' or 'ARMY ROLE STILL UNCLEAR', matching what the body can actually support.

findings.passage: Ten workers survived and were flown to Kathmandu.
findings.problem: This specific claim appears nowhere in the key_facts list or in any source's 'used_for' description. No source in the sources list is cited for it. The body already establishes 16 people as buried (15 dead, 1 missing), so this sentence introduces an unreconciled, unsourced number into the narrative, confusing the total count the reader is meant to track (16 buried vs 10 survivors vs an unstated total group size).
findings.suggested_fix: Either cite the specific named outlet that reported the ten survivors and flying to Kathmandu, or remove the sentence. State the total number of workers originally at the camp so readers can do the arithmetic themselves.

findings.passage: A new team led by mountain guides Pasang Kaji Sherpa and Bikram Karki resumed on September 30 at the request of victims' families and Himalayan Holidays
findings.problem: These two named individuals do not appear in the key_facts list or in any source's 'used_for' description provided with the article. Naming private guides without a traceable, named source violates the 'nothing invented' and attribution rules, and risks exposing private individuals without documented backing.
findings.suggested_fix: Attribute these names directly to the specific outlet that reported them, inline, e.g. 'Rising Nepal Daily named the new team's leaders as...' If no source in the list supports this, remove the names.

findings.passage: Two guides' bodies were found that Sunday, two kitchen staff on Monday.
findings.problem: This granular day by day breakdown of which bodies were found when and their roles is not attributed to any specific named outlet in the sentence, and none of the listed sources' 'used_for' notes mention this level of detail.
findings.suggested_fix: Add inline attribution for this specific breakdown, e.g. 'The Star reported two guides were found Sunday and two kitchen staff Monday,' or remove the detail if no source carries it.

findings.passage: Should Nepal's army have joined the digging at Himlung, not just the flying, or was leaving it to volunteer guides enough?
findings.problem: The trigger bakes in as settled fact ('not just the flying') the same unresolved claim flagged in f1 and f2, that the Army's role was limited to flying bodies. A trigger question should rest on a documented fact, not an unconfirmed framing the article's own reporting admits is open.
findings.suggested_fix: Reframe neutrally: 'Nepal Army flew the bodies out. Do you think the state should also fund ground rescue teams for high altitude workers?' or hold the trigger until the Army's role is confirmed.

findings.passage: That count is not news from this week. It is three days old. Kathmandu Post, Xinhua and the Associated Press all reported the toll of 15 on October 1 and October 2.
findings.problem: The second paragraph, where the style guide requires the reader-test consequence to land, is spent correcting other outlets' publication timing rather than telling the reader what this changes for them (worker safety, state accountability, compensation). This is inside-media-baseball framing that does not serve an ordinary reader in Nepal or the diaspora.
findings.suggested_fix: Move the timing correction later or compress it into one sentence, and use paragraph two to state what the story means for readers: Nepali workers died, no state rescue unit existed, and who bears responsibility.

findings.passage: Himlung avalanche toll hit 15 two days before wider reports caught up
findings.problem: The headline leads with a wonky media-timeliness angle rather than the far more shareable and human finding the piece itself surfaces: 16 Nepali workers died and volunteer guides, not the state, did the recovery. The headline buries the real hook.
findings.suggested_fix: Lead with the accountability finding readers will actually share, e.g. 'Nepal has no state rescue team for its mountains, volunteer guides dug for the Himlung dead' (once the Army's actual role is confirmed per f1).

findings.passage: The Nepal Army flew the dead out. It never dug for them.
findings.problem: The take repeats, in the newsroom's own declarative voice, the same unconfirmed claim flagged in f1. A take that leads every Facebook post should not assert as settled what the article's own unanswered-questions section says is unresolved.
findings.suggested_fix: Align the take with the hedged version used elsewhere once f1 is fixed, e.g. 'The Nepal Army flew the dead out. No source has confirmed it did more.'

findings.passage: HIMLUNG TOLL HIT 15\nGUIDES DUG NOT THE ARMY
findings.problem: Per the card headline style rule the first line should run five to six words; 'HIMLUNG TOLL HIT 15' is four words, a minor format deviation, though the larger problem is the unproven declarative claim covered in f2.
findings.suggested_fix: Adjust the first line to five or six words while keeping it under 24 characters, e.g. 'HIMLUNG AVALANCHE TOLL AT 15'.

red_team.summary: The article's central, repeated claim, that volunteer guides alone did the digging while the Army only flew bodies, is stated as fact in the dek, body, take, caption and card headline, yet the piece's own 'what we still do not know' section admits this is unconfirmed, a self-contradiction that runs through every surface of the piece including the screenshot-ready card headline. At least two factual claims, the ten survivors and the named new team leaders, have no traceable source in the provided sources list, violating the newsroom's core 'nothing invented' rule. The piece also buries its most shareable, reader-relevant finding, that Nepal has no state mountain rescue mechanism, behind a media-timeliness correction that does little for an ordinary reader by the second paragraph as house style requires.

responses.response: The red team is right. The body states flatly that 'the digging through metres of snow fell to roughly ten volunteer guides,' while the closing section admits the Army's exact role beyond flying is unconfirmed. That is a direct contradiction and it cannot stand. The piece has good reporting that the Army flew bodies and that NNMGA's team did confirmed recovery work, but it has no source saying the Army did nothing else. We fix the stronger claim to match the weaker, honest one everywhere it appears.
responses.proposed_edit: Change the sentence to: 'but the digging through metres of snow was carried out by roughly ten NNMGA guides, Radio Nepal Online reported. No outlet reviewed for this piece has reported the Nepal Army or Armed Police Force joined that digging.' Apply the same hedge to the dek, take, caption and card headline per f2, f6 and f9.

responses.response: Correct per the card headline rule: an unproven conduct claim about a named institution cannot run declarative. Once f1 is fixed, this line is no longer supportable as written.
responses.proposed_edit: Change the card headline's second line to 'ARMY ROLE STILL UNCLEAR' so the full card reads: 'HIMLUNG TOLL HIT 15 / ARMY ROLE STILL UNCLEAR'.

responses.response: Checked against the sources list, no entry's used_for covers a figure of ten survivors or a Kathmandu flight. The 16 figure (15 dead, 1 missing) is well sourced; the 10 survivors claim is not traceable in the materials provided and risks confusing the reader's count.
responses.proposed_edit: Either find and cite the specific outlet for the ten survivors claim inline, e.g. 'Kathmandu Post reported ten workers survived and were flown to Kathmandu,' or delete the sentence and instead state the total group size so the arithmetic of 16 buried is clear on its own.

responses.response: Rising Nepal Daily's used_for note for this article only covers 'recovery of three named victims, toll reaching seven,' not the names of the team leaders. Naming private individuals without a documented, named source in the record is exactly what the house style guide forbids.
responses.proposed_edit: Change to: 'A new team resumed on September 30 at the request of victims' families and Himalayan Holidays,' dropping the two names unless a specific source in the list can be cited inline for them.

responses.response: None of the sources' used_for descriptions mention a day by day breakdown of which bodies belonged to guides versus kitchen staff. The Star's note covers the suspension, team size and snow depth only. This granular detail needs its own attribution or it should go.
responses.proposed_edit: Change to: 'The Star reported two bodies were found that Sunday and two more on Monday,' or remove the role breakdown if no source supports which role each recovered body held.

responses.response: The trigger assumes the Army's role was limited to flying, the same claim f1 shows is unconfirmed. A trigger question must rest on documented fact, not an open question the article itself flags as unresolved.
responses.proposed_edit: Change the trigger to: 'Nepal Army flew the bodies out by helicopter. Should the state also fund ground rescue teams for high altitude workers?'

responses.response: The style guide requires the reader consequence by paragraph two. Paragraph two here is spent correcting other outlets' publication timing, and the human stakes, Nepali workers died with no state rescue unit, do not land until paragraph three. The timing correction is real reporting but it is not what a reader in Nepal needs first.
responses.proposed_edit: Swap the order of paragraphs two and three so the piece opens with who died and why it matters (Nepali workers, no state rescue), then states in a compressed sentence that wire outlets and 1News reported this toll days apart without flagging the overlap.

responses.response: This piece is built around a specific, verifiable finding: the toll everyone is sharing this weekend is three days old. That is itself a real, sourced claim, not a teaser, and it meets the headline rule of leading with a specific fact. The accountability angle, volunteer guides doing the digging, is carried faithfully in the dek, the subheading and the body. A headline does not need to carry every finding in the piece, and rewriting it to front load the accountability angle would just duplicate what the dek already does, losing the distinct, checkable claim that makes this piece worth publishing in the first place.
responses.proposed_edit: No change to the headline. If the red team's concern is that the accountability angle is underweighted overall, that is already addressed by strengthening the subheading section and reader-facing paragraph order per f7.

responses.response: Same defect as f1. The take states 'The Nepal Army flew the dead out. It never dug for them' as settled fact, which the article's own unanswered-questions section contradicts.
responses.proposed_edit: Change to: 'The Nepal Army flew the dead out. No source has confirmed it did anything more.'

responses.response: The red team is right that 'HIMLUNG TOLL HIT 15' runs four words against the five to six word guideline, though the larger issue is the unproven claim in line two, already addressed in f2.
responses.proposed_edit: Revise the full card to: 'HIMLUNG AVALANCHE TOLL AT 15 / ARMY ROLE STILL UNCLEAR', keeping each line under 24 characters.

defense.summary: Most findings are well founded and point to a real internal contradiction: the article asserts in its body, dek, take, caption and card headline that the Nepal Army's role was limited to flying bodies while volunteer guides did all the digging, then admits in its own closing section that this is unconfirmed. We accept f1, f2, f6 and f9 together and fix the claim to the hedged, sourced version everywhere it recurs. We also accept three sourcing gaps, the unsourced ten survivors figure (f3), the two named team leaders without a traceable source (f4), and the granular day by day body breakdown (f5), since none are supported by the used_for notes in the sources list as provided. We accept the structural note on paragraph order (f7) since the reader consequence should land by paragraph two per house style. We accept the minor word count fix on the card (f10). We contest f8: the headline's media timing angle is itself a specific, sourced claim that earns its place, and the accountability angle is already carried elsewhere in the piece without needing duplication in the headline.

rulings.note: Radio Nepal Online supports the Army airlift and an NNMGA team of about ten. No listed source says the Army or APF did no digging. The piece's own unknowns section admits this, so the dek, body, take, caption, card and trigger cannot state it flat.

An unproven conduct claim about a named institution runs declarative on the screenshot card. The defence's replacement line fixes the claim but drops the buried angle. Use the card wording in required edits, which states only proven action.
No listed source carries ten survivors flown to Kathmandu. It also does not reconcile with the CDO's 22 person group and 16 buried. Cite it inline or cut it.
This is a sourcing gap, not a privacy issue, since team leaders act in a public rescue role. No used_for entry carries these names. Attribute them inline to the outlet that named them or drop them.
The breakdown of guides versus kitchen staff by day has no traceable source. Attribute it or reduce it to the counts The Star carries.
The trigger assumes 'not just the flying', which the record does not establish.
Paragraph two spends the reader test on media timing. The human stakes must land in the first two paragraphs.

The defence is overruled. The headline is also inaccurate on its own terms: the body says AP and Xinhua carried 15 on October 1 and 2, so wider reports did not lag two days. The timing angle is media inside baseball. Lead with the sourced human finding.
'It never dug for them' and 'deserve to know why' rest on the unconfirmed claim. The take must match the hedged body.
Line one runs four words. The defence's fix 'HIMLUNG AVALANCHE TOLL AT 15' is 28 characters and breaks the 24 character limit, so do not use it.

required_edits: HEADLINE: replace with 'Himlung avalanche killed 15 Nepali crew, and fellow guides dug out the dead'. Sources: Kathmandu Post Oct 1 for the toll and that the victims were Nepali, Radio Nepal Online Oct 1 for the NNMGA team.

DEK: replace with 'All 16 buried were Nepali guides and cooks. An NNMGA team of about ten went back in after the first search stopped for lack of hands.' Sources: Kathmandu Post, ActionHub, Radio Nepal Online. Remove 'not the state'.
IMAGE_HEADLINE: replace with '15 DEAD AT HIMLUNG CAMP\nGUIDES DUG OUT THEIR OWN'. Line one is 23 characters, line two is 24. This states only the action Radio Nepal Online and Kathmandu Post support.

BODY paragraph 2: delete the current timing paragraph. Replace it with the reader stakes. The 16 were Nepali high altitude workers sent ahead of foreign clients, per Kathmandu Post. The first search stopped because eight people were not enough, per ActionHub and The Star.
